title: Members who borrowed every classic
prompt:
A community library flags some books as classics. The reading club wants to reward members who have borrowed every classic at least once.

Return each member who has at least one loan of every book where is_classic is true.

- Columns: id, name
- Any row order is fine
- Borrowing the same classic twice counts once
- Loans of non-classic books do not matter
- If the library has no classics at all, return no rows
hints: This is relational division: members whose set of borrowed classics equals the full set of classics.
Count how many distinct classics each member borrowed and compare with how many classics exist.
Join loans to books filtered on is_classic, GROUP BY member, and use HAVING count(DISTINCT b.id) = (SELECT count(*) FROM books WHERE is_classic).

exercise.starter:
-- Members who borrowed every classic
SELECT DISTINCT m.id, m.name
FROM members m
JOIN loans l ON l.member_id = m.id
JOIN books b ON b.id = l.book_id AND b.is_classic;
exercise.solution:
SELECT m.id, m.name
FROM members m
JOIN loans l ON l.member_id = m.id
JOIN books b ON b.id = l.book_id AND b.is_classic
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
HAVING count(DISTINCT b.id) = (SELECT count(*) FROM books WHERE is_classic);

tests.name: one member completes the set
two members complete the set

hiddenTests.name: repeat loans count once
no classics means no winners
extra non-classic loans are fine
single classic and a member with no loans

explanation: Filtering the join to classics and counting distinct classic ids per member gives the size of each member's borrowed set; a member qualifies when it equals the number of classics. count(DISTINCT b.id) matters because a member who borrowed one classic twice would otherwise look like they borrowed two. When there are no classics, the join produces no groups, so no rows come back, as the prompt requires. The double NOT EXISTS form (no classic that this member has not borrowed) is the other classic answer, but it is vacuously true for every member when the set is empty, so it needs an extra guard here.
notes: The counting form is usually one hash join plus a hash aggregate, and the scalar subquery runs once. Indexes on loans(member_id, book_id) help the double NOT EXISTS form, which Postgres plans as nested anti joins. If the required set comes from user input, pass it as an array or VALUES list and compare counts the same way.
followUps: Rewrite it with double NOT EXISTS and add the guard for an empty set of classics.
